one_liner: Reference bzip2/libbz2: Burrows-Wheeler compressor whose decoder is 2.5-14x faster than PPMd at a similar ratio, but slow by modern standards.
what_it_does: libbz2 is the reference library and CLI for the .bz2 format: block-sorting compression in independent 100-900 KB blocks with a CRC32 per block and per stream. The API is zlib-like (BZ2_bzCompressInit/BZ2_bzCompress/BZ2_bzDecompress on a bz_stream, one-shot BZ2_bzBuffToBuffCompress/Decompress, and a stdio FILE layer). It is not a drop-in for PPMd or any other format; its value is reading and writing the .bz2 files that every Unix toolchain and distribution already ships. This GitLab project is the archived 1.1 development fork; release 1.0.8 is maintained at sourceware, and the compression and decompression sources here match lzbench's 1.0.8 copy apart from whitespace and version strings.
how_it_is_fast: Against PPM the speed comes from the transform, not tuning: an initial run-length pass, a Burrows-Wheeler transform (radix pre-sort plus multikey quicksort in mainSort, with a fallbackSort when a work budget runs out on repetitive data), move-to-front, zero-run coding and up to 6 canonical Huffman tables switched every 50 symbols. Decoding is Huffman decoding plus an inverse BWT that walks one 4-bytes-per-symbol array (BZ_GET_FAST), which is far cheaper than PPMd's per-symbol context modelling and range decoding, so the decoder wins even though PPM is symmetric. The decoder still looks up Huffman code lengths bit by bit and chases cache-missing pointers, which is why it decodes at 35.5 MB/s while LZ decoders run at hundreds.
when_to_use: You must read or write .bz2 (tarballs, archives, scientific and genomics files, legacy pipelines); libbz2 is the system library on essentially every Linux distribution.

Text-like data where you want a better ratio than zlib (25.75% vs 31.92% for zlib 1.3.2 -9 on silesia.tar) with small, bounded memory: about 7.6 MB to compress and 3.7 MB to decompress at -9, or 2.3 MB with the small decoder.

When you are choosing between bzip2 and a PPM codec and decode speed matters: bzip2 -9 decodes 3.1x faster than ppmd8 -4 and 2.5x faster than ppmd8 -1 at a 2% smaller output than the latter (lzbench 2.4, derived from page data).
Embedded or constrained builds: the low-level interface is plain C89 with no globals and can be built with -DBZ_NO_STDIO.
when_not_to_use: Any new format choice: in the same lzbench 2.4 table zstd 1.5.7 -18 is 2.4% smaller and decodes 33x faster (1175 vs 35.5 MB/s, though it compresses 3.1x slower), lzma 26.03 -4 is 2.5% larger but compresses 1.07x and decodes 2.1x faster, and lzma -9 is 10.8% smaller and decodes 2.2x faster (derived from page data).
When you need the best BWT ratio: bsc 3.3.12 -m0 -e1 is 9.7% smaller and compresses 1.5x faster, bzip3 1.5.4 -5 is 13.4% smaller (both decode slower than bzip2).
When you need bzip2-format speed: lbzip2 2.6.5 -9 writes the same format at the same size and is 1.76x faster to compress and 1.32x faster to decompress on one thread, and it parallelizes.

Multi-core or random access: libbz2 is single-threaded and the format does not record compressed block sizes, so parallel decoding means scanning for block magic (the manual names this as a format flaw; GitLab issues #11 parallel compression and #12 faster BWT stay open).
Small messages or latency-sensitive paths: blocks are 100-900 KB and the BWT needs the whole block before output.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (libbz2; Meson or CMake on the 1.1 master branch, classic Makefile in the 1.0.8 release)
integration.min_toolchain: C89 (meson default c_std=c89); Meson 0.56+ or CMake 3.12+ for the 1.1 master build
integration.platforms: any (portable C; Unix, Windows via CMake/nmake, MinGW with open build issues)
integration.thread_safety: Low-level BZ2_bzCompress/BZ2_bzDecompress interface has no globals and is thread-safe per stream (manual); the high-level stdio layer reports I/O errors through errno, and the zlib-compatible bzopen/bzread/bzwrite functions are marked untested and not checked for thread safety.

gotchas: Use 1.0.8 or later: 1.0.7 fixed CVE-2019-12900 (nSelectors out of range in the decoder, found by fuzzing) and CVE-2016-3189 (use-after-free in bzip2recover); the 1.0.7 fix rejected some lbzip2-written files and 1.0.8 relaxed it (GitLab issue #24).
BZ2_bzBuffToBuffCompress/Decompress take unsigned int lengths, so one-shot calls are limited to under 4 GB; use the streaming API for larger data.

Highly repetitive input can make compression up to about 10x slower than average (manual); the fallback sort is about 3x slower than the main sort, and workFactor (default 30) controls when it kicks in. Decompression speed is unaffected.

The 1.1 master branch changes the Linux SONAME to libbz2.so.1 (1.0 used libbz2.so.1.0; CMake -DUSE_OLD_SONAME=ON builds both) and ships no Makefile (open issue #60); the archived GitLab fork will not get fixes, so take release code from sourceware.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libbz2 only when the .bz2 format is required and you want the canonical, distro-shipped implementation; for bzip2-format speed lbzip2 is faster on one core and scales across cores, and for anything format-free zstd, xz/LZMA or bzip3/libbsc beat it on ratio, speed or both.
verified_claims_summary: lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 -O3 release binary, one thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off, silesia.tar) measured bzip2 1.0.8 -9 at 12.7 MB/s compress, 35.5 MB/s decompress and 54,572,811 bytes, versus 7-Zip ppmd8 26.03 -4 at 12.8/11.5 MB/s and 51,241,932 bytes and ppmd8 -1 at 15.7/14.0 MB/s and 55,803,295 bytes: about 3.1x and 2.5x faster decoding with equal or slower compression (derived from page data). lzbench's ppmd8 levels map to small models (level L uses order 3+L and 2^(L-1) MB, so -1 is an order-4, 1 MB model reset whenever memory fills), and every run is checked by memcmp against the input.
status_note: The GitLab 1.1 fork is archived ('lack of interest, and because there are better options available through the Rust ecosystem', last commit 2023-05-31) while 1.0.8 (2019) lives on at sourceware; usability is reference because SPDX marks the permissive BSD-style bzip2-1.0.6 licence as not OSI-approved, though it is free to use, small C89 and universally packaged.
